slides.title: Horus connector assessment
slides.kicker: Chift product/tech case · Part 1 · Mapping Chift – Horus
slides.lead: Can Chift's accounting routes be served from the Horus Software API, and what must be confirmed before building?

items.text: Prepared by Silas Deblanc for Chift, Product & Tech
13 October 2026 · Status: for discussion
Basis: desk analysis of the documentation, no live API calls

slides.callout: Proposals are analysis, not commitments on behalf of Chift or Horus.
slides.notes: Thanks for having me. In about twenty minutes I'll cover four things. First, the answer: what the documentation confirms and what it doesn't. Second, how Horus differs from Chift, because most of the work comes from those differences. Third, Task A, the route mapping, and Task B, the attribute mapping for client creation, invoice creation and outstanding items. Finally, what your clients would notice, the decisions that are yours, the questions for Horus, and my recommendation. This is a desk analysis: no live API calls were sent, and anything I call a proposal is mine to discuss, not an agreed rule. Questions are welcome at the end.

slides.title: One five-step method answered both tasks, route by route
slides.lead: Two levels of mapping, built with the same method for every route.

items.text: Horus endpoints and specificities for 10 Chift routes
Every attribute and query parameter of 3 routes
One Chift route may need several Horus endpoints
Explain the result so Chift's clients can follow it, in plain language

blocks.heading: Method, the same for every route

items.text: Read both contracts in full for the routes in scope
Align vocabulary: each Chift term and its Horus equivalent
Ask the same questions per route: object, calls, fields, what is lost
Label every claim: Documented, Derived, Assumption, To confirm
Check each mapping against the docs, then challenge it in a critical review

slides.callout: Sources: the case, Chift's OpenAPI spec, Horus reference and guides, two VAT spreadsheets · no live API calls
slides.notes: The case asked two things. Task A: for ten Chift routes, which Horus endpoints to use and what to watch. Task B: for three routes, client creation, invoice creation and outstanding items, every attribute and query parameter. It also hinted that one Chift route may need several Horus calls, and that turned out to be central. My method was the same for every route: read both contracts, align the vocabulary, ask the same questions, label every claim by its evidence, then challenge the result in a critical review. That review changed some conclusions; the first backup slide lists the main ones. Likely question: why not test the API? There was no test licence, and Horus requests run on real data.

slides.title: Nothing is ruled out, but only one route is fully confirmed
slides.lead: 11 routes: the ten of Task A plus outstanding items. Proposal: validate before building.
slides.callout: Not concluded for any list route: behaviour on large folders (no documented limits, no volume test run).
slides.notes: I looked at eleven routes: the ten of Task A plus outstanding items from Task B. Horus has a documented endpoint for the core object of every route, so the documentation rules nothing out. Only analytic accounts is fully confirmed. Six rest on assumptions the docs don't confirm. Four need answers from Horus or decisions from Chift; likely your clients' highest-value routes, to confirm with you. For every list route, I can't conclude how it behaves on large folders. Hence my proposal: validate first, not a full build. Likely question: 'So is it feasible?' The documentation rules nothing out, but only one route is confirmed: six rest on assumptions, four designs aren't final, and large-folder behaviour can't be concluded yet.

slides.title: Core capabilities are documented; VAT, read rules and volumes remain open
slides.lead: Four evidence levels, from documented to not yet decidable.

VAT spreadsheets are current, and the API accepts the Luxembourg origins

Horus, reads: ledger currency, limits, partial matching
Chift: posting mode, unnumbered invoices, caching, currency conversion
Performance and completeness of list routes on large folders

slides.callout: Also before build: Horus access, test licence, confirmation rights, docs version (H17, H19–H21, H24)
slides.notes: This slide sorts the evidence into four levels. First, what the documentation states: endpoints for every route, native invoice posting, native client open items. Second, what rests on my assumptions; for example, that lists return complete results, which I deduced from the absence of paging parameters. Third, questions with an owner: Horus on VAT, credit notes, numbering, currency, limits and partial matching; Chift on posting mode, numbering, caching and currency conversion. Horus access and a test licence also come before build. Last, what I can't conclude yet, mainly large folders. Likely question: 'What's riskiest?' VAT first, then posting and numbering, then untested volumes on large folders; on reads, credit notes and partly paid supplier invoices.

slides.title: One Chift call often means several Horus calls
slides.kicker: How Horus differs · Worked example: invoice creation
slides.lead: Horus needs its own references first, and a create returns only an id.

blocks.heading: Look up references, cached per folder

items.text: Why: Horus posts by its own codes; folder legislation selects the VAT list

blocks.heading: Check the partner's folder and role

items.text: Why: Horus needs a CompanyId; whether it checks folder and role is undocumented (H11)
Why: no documented safe retry, and invoices cannot be deleted via the API

blocks.heading: Post to the sales or purchase endpoint, PDF included

items.text: Why: one native call per invoice or credit note; Horus returns only an id
Why: stored number, status and update date come only from Horus

slides.callout: Same pattern on reads: no endpoint lists all invoices, so invoice retrieval is rebuilt from ledger data.
slides.notes: This is the pattern behind most routes, shown on invoice creation. Chift sends one request. Before posting, the connector needs Horus's own references: the daybook, the accounts, the analytic codes, and the folder's legislation, which selects the VAT list. Those are cached per folder, but fiscal years are read fresh, because the accountant can close a period at any time. Then it checks the partner and, as a best-effort proposal, whether the number already exists. The create returns only an id, so we read the entry back. Likely question: 'Why so many calls?' Most are cached reference data, and a wrong invoice can't be deleted through the API, so checking first is cheaper.

slides.title: Similar words mean different things in Chift and Horus
slides.lead: Horus has its own vocabulary and rules; most effort and risk come from these differences, not from missing objects.

slides.callout: In Horus, a 'company' is a customer or supplier inside a folder, never the folder's own company.
slides.notes: Most mapping mistakes come from words that look alike. In Horus, a 'company' is a third party the folder deals with, a customer or supplier, not the folder's own company. One record can be both, which is why Chift's force_merge fits well. A journal is a daybook, and its type decides which endpoint can post into it. Analytic plans are cost schemas, and Horus stores amounts on combinations, not percentages. There is no VAT-code entity at all. And pairing 'posted' with 'confirmed' is my proposal, not something the documentation states. Likely question: 'Why not map posted to confirmed directly?' Horus keeps API entries unconfirmed for the accountant's review; that's Chift's call, C1.

slides.title: Every route maps to a main Horus endpoint plus supporting calls
slides.lead: The ten Task A routes, plus outstanding items from Task B.
slides.callout: '+ N' counts supporting endpoints, not calls per request · build effort is the analyst's estimate, to calibrate with Chift
slides.notes: This table answers Task A, plus outstanding items from Task B. For each route: the main Horus endpoint, and a '+ N' count of supporting endpoints for reference data, checks and read-backs. That count is endpoints, not calls per request. Most Horus filtered lists use POST with the filters in the body; most simple reads by id use GET. The feasibility column rates each route by evidence, by its weakest material point; the last column, build effort, is my estimate, to calibrate with you. Details are in section 3 of the report. Likely question: 'Which route is simplest?' By effort, folders, journals, analytic plans and analytic accounts are low; by evidence, analytic accounts is the only fully confirmed route.

slides.title: Reference routes are mostly single calls, but five rest on assumptions
slides.lead: Five rest on interpreting undocumented Horus data; only analytic accounts is fully confirmed.

blocks.heading: Reads: journals, chart of accounts, folders

items.text: Journals: one call lists every daybook; blocked and currency flags rest on assumptions (H14)
Chart of accounts: number, name, status native; account type is a computed estimate (H12)
Folders: id, name, VAT number, address native; currency (EUR) and active status assumed
Ledger account creation: number and name documented; returned type is the chart's estimate
Analytic plans: one call; parent plan field undocumented; free-text dimensions hidden (Proposal, C9)
Analytic accounts: documented loop over up to eight plans; no stored balances (C4)

slides.callout: Build effort (analyst's estimate): low for journals, folders, analytic plans and accounts; medium for chart and ledger accounts.
slides.notes: These six routes are the reference data most other routes depend on; most are a single Horus call, cached per folder. The ratings are by evidence, not effort. Five are 'feasible with assumptions' because part of the response rests on an interpretation of undocumented Horus data, such as the account type, the folder currency, or the parent of an analytic plan. Analytic accounts is confirmed; Horus simply stores no balances, and how to show them is a Chift question, C4. Effort is my estimate, to calibrate with you. Likely question: 'Why isn't the chart of accounts confirmed?' Horus has no account type, so the Chift type is computed from several sources.

slides.title: Four routes carry the effort and the open questions
slides.lead: None is ruled out, but all four wait on Horus answers or Chift decisions.

Numbers must be numeric; entries unconfirmed by default; no invoice delete via API
**Waits on:** H1 VAT files · H3 numbering · C1 posting · C7 numbering

slides.callout: Proposal: build invoice creation and operations after the reference routes; ledger-based reads wait for Horus's answers.
slides.notes: These four routes carry most of the effort and most of the open questions. Invoice creation is native in Horus, but VAT, numbering and posting status need answers first. Invoice retrieval is the most complex read: no endpoint lists all invoices, so we rebuild them from the ledger, and telling invoices from credit notes rests on my proposed rule, H2. Miscellaneous operations have no currency field, so who converts is your decision, C15. For outstanding items, the supplier side depends on how Horus returns partially matched lines, H8. Likely question: 'Why is retrieval harder than creation?' Creation is native; retrieval has no full invoice list, so each invoice is assembled from several Horus lists.

slides.title: About two in three attributes map directly, by transform or lookup
slides.kicker: Task B · Attributes and query parameters
slides.lead: The effort sits in a few places: VAT codes, the client code, unstorable fields.
slides.callout: 'Not available' is not blocked: unstorable inputs are rejected or dropped (Chift decides, C3); missing outputs return null.
slides.notes: Task B goes down to every attribute and query parameter of three routes. Each bar shows how the rows split by mapping type. About two in three map directly or by a transform or lookup. The effort sits in a few places: the VAT-code lookup, the client search key the connector must generate, and fields Horus can't store, like line quantity or extra addresses. 'Not available' doesn't mean blocked: for inputs, Chift decides whether to reject or drop them, C3; missing outputs come back null. Likely question: what is 'filled by connector or Chift'? Values Horus doesn't supply: a generated correction line, fixed values such as an empty payments list, and the paging and totals that Chift handles.

slides.callout: Writes go to real data, and the API has no call to delete a company (test folder: H17)
slides.notes: For client creation, the key idea is that Horus keeps one record per third party, the 'company', flagged as customer and/or supplier. So a Chift client becomes a company flagged as customer, and force_merge adds that flag to an existing supplier. The flow is check, create, read back, build, because Horus returns only an id. The real business choice is the search key: Horus requires it, Chift never sends it, and accountants see it as the client's code. My proposal is to derive it from the name, but Chift should agree the convention. Likely question: what if a client is sent twice? Without a VAT number or external reference, there is no reliable duplicate check.

slides.notes: Invoice creation is native in Horus: one endpoint for sales, one for purchases, invoices and credit notes, with the PDF in the same call. The call flow is the one from the worked example, so I'll focus on the table. The account number is Direct, not Lookup, because Horus posts on the account number itself. tax_code is a Lookup into a Horus VAT combination, which is the next slide. Quantity is simply not stored. Likely question: how do analytic percentages become amounts? Line base times percentage, rounded so the cost lines add up to the base: a 1,000 euro line split 60/40 gives 600 and 400. The exact rounding rule I'd settle with engineering.

slides.notes: This is the most important transformation. Chift sends one tax_code per invoice line, the id of a VAT code. Horus has no such code: each line carries a rate, an origin and a type, plus kind and condition on purchases, and only the combinations in two published spreadsheets are accepted; the counts are on the slide. My proposal is that the connector owns a VAT-code list per folder legislation and direction, and rejects unknown codes before calling Horus. The spreadsheets and the API reference disagree in places, which is why H1 is the first question for Horus. Likely question: why not use the VatCode Horus returns on read? Its meaning is undocumented, so that is part of H1.

slides.title: Client open items are native; supplier open amounts must be computed
slides.lead: The `type` parameter picks the Horus lists: two for clients, one for suppliers.

items.text: Open sales invoices list: native open amount, due date, invoice currency
Joined with customer ledger lines for account and matching number
Open invoices keep their currency; other lines in EUR, so currencies can mix (C16, H4)
No purchase-side open-invoice list: only supplier ledger lines
Connector computes open amounts from unmatched lines (Credit − Debit)
Partly paid invoices depend on H8; otherwise a fallback ledger read

slides.callout: `page` and `size` are emulated on the full set (H5, C14) · signs are a proposal (C5)
slides.notes: Outstanding items show the asymmetry best, and the query parameters drive it. The type parameter picks the Horus source. For clients, Horus has a ready list of open sales invoices with a documented open amount; we join it with customer ledger lines for the account and matching number. For suppliers there is no equivalent, so the connector computes open amounts from unmatched ledger lines. If partially matched lines aren't returned, partly paid supplier invoices silently disappear, which is why H8 is before build. With unposted_allowed=false, only confirmed entries come back, so API-pushed entries stay out until the accountant confirms them. Likely question: one call per supplier? No, if leaving out the company filter returns every partner, also H8.

slides.callout: Withholding tax, the Dutch G/N split and a forced period in another month: rejected (proposal, C3); a delivery date in another month: Chift decides (C3, H10)
slides.notes: I'd share this slide with a client application team. In one sentence: invoices you push may wait for the accountant's review, numbers must be numeric, and line quantities and extra addresses stay on your side. The biggest friction is review: a vendor used to 'posted' will see drafts until the accountant confirms, unless Chift chooses direct posting. A pushed invoice can't be deleted through the integration, and an edit comes back with a new id. The currency row stays a proposal until Horus answers H4. Likely question: what's hardest to explain? The new id after an edit: it breaks stored references; matching on journal and number plus periodic re-syncs limits the impact, but unnumbered entries stay hard to find.

slides.title: Five Chift decisions shape what the connector promises clients
slides.lead: Each proposal is a starting point for discussion, not an agreed rule.

items.text: Review first, or confirm directly?
Mode per connection, review by default; return the status actually stored
Confirmation looks like accountant validation (H21); no invoice delete via the API
Reject non-numeric numbers? And unnumbered invoices?
Reject non-numeric; an unnumbered invoice goes to review as a draft
Horus stores numbers as numbers and does not number API invoices
Cache between pages? Which timeout?
Cache reference data per folder and results between page calls
Horus lists cannot be paged; without a cache, every page re-reads the period
Who converts operations to EUR: Chift core or connector?
Convert at the supplied rate rather than reject; original currency not kept
Horus operation lines have no currency field; Chift requires a rate
Accept a connector-built list?
One list per legislation and direction; null on read when ambiguous
Horus accepts published VAT combinations, not codes

slides.notes: These are decisions I cannot make for Chift: they change what Chift promises its clients and how the connector behaves next to other connectors. Each comes with a proposal to start the discussion. C1 is the most visible: Chift defaults to 'posted', while Horus keeps API entries unconfirmed for the accountant. C7 follows from Horus storing numbers as numbers. C14 and C15 are platform questions; C2 decides the VAT approach. Likely question: why review by default? Invoices cannot be deleted through the API at all, so the accountant's review is the last check, and it is how Horus is designed. Under my proposal direct posting stays available per connection, provided Horus confirms every user may confirm through the API, H21.

slides.notes: These are the before-build questions for Horus, grouped so they are easy to send as one list. If I could ask only four first: are the VAT spreadsheets current, what are the limits and can we get a test licence, how do numbering and retries work, and how are partial matches returned for suppliers. The access questions come first in time, because registration and a test folder unlock every other check. Likely question: why is H20 there? The case links the older apiary documentation; I used the current docs and did not compare the two, so Horus should confirm which one is authoritative.

slides.callout: A proposal for Chift's decision, not a commitment on behalf of Chift or Horus
slides.notes: My recommendation is deliberately cautious. Gate 0 comes first: send the questions, get a test licence, settle Chift's decisions. Phase 1 builds the reference routes and simple creates, which also prove the connection, the caching and the response times. Phase 2 adds the creates where VAT and numbering matter. Phase 3 holds the reads that carry most open questions. Throughout, the Task B tables serve as acceptance criteria, and every confirmed answer updates the detailed reference. The fallbacks keep the plan alive if answers disappoint. Likely question: how long will it take? I gave relative effort per route, low, medium or high, but no days: that depends on Chift's connector framework and on Horus's answers.

slides.notes: To close: Horus has a documented endpoint for the core object of every route, so nothing is ruled out, but only analytic accounts is fully confirmed, and large-folder behaviour can't be concluded yet for any list route. The effort and the risk sit in VAT, posting and numbering, and the reads rebuilt from the ledger. So my proposal is to validate first and build in phases. The concise report is the position I defend; the detailed reference holds the full mapping. Likely question: you changed your conclusion between versions? Yes. I reviewed my own work against the documentation and separated what is documented from what I assumed. The material corrections are listed in appendix B.

slides.callout: Appendix B of the report lists all 18 changes, with the reason for each
slides.notes: I include this because the conclusion changed between versions, and I would rather show it than have it found. After the first version I challenged my own work as a senior reviewer would. The headline moved from 'all feasible' to a split by evidence. I found the Horus VAT spreadsheets I had first missed. And several implementation rules became proposals or open questions, such as the posting default and the credit-note rule on read. The detailed reference is kept as the record; the concise report is the position I defend. Likely question: does this mean the reference is wrong? Where they differ, the concise report and appendix B apply.

slides.notes: For transparency on evidence. I used the current Horus documentation, while the case links the older apiary version; the two were not compared, which is question H20. The Chift contract comes from the OpenAPI file bundled in the Python SDK, because docs.chift.eu was not reachable, so Chift should confirm nothing important has changed. Every statement carries a label, and proposals are marked as such. Likely question: what separates Derived from Assumption? Derived is deduced from the documentation, for example that lists return complete results, because no list has paging parameters. An assumption is my interpretation or proposal, which Horus or Chift must confirm.
